questions.question_text: A broker signs a listing agreement with a homeowner in Seattle. Under RCW 18.86, what is the broker's role?
questions.explanation: A firm that signs a listing agreement appoints the broker as the seller's agent (RCW 18.86.020(1)(a)). Washington's duties are statutory, not fiduciary: RCW 18.86.110 states they are "statutory duties and not fiduciary duties" and "supersedes the fiduciary duties of an agent to a principal under the common law." On top of the duties owed to all parties in RCW 18.86.030, a seller's agent owes the seller loyalty, timely disclosure of conflicts, advice to seek expert help beyond the agent's expertise, confidentiality, and a good faith and continuous effort to find a buyer (RCW 18.86.040(1)).

questions.question_text: A buyer hires a broker to help purchase a condo in Tacoma. Which statement best describes the broker's obligation?
questions.correct_answer: Statutory buyer-agency duties to the buyer
distractors: Equal duties to buyer and seller
Duties only when an offer is written
questions.explanation: Under RCW 18.86.020(1) a broker who performs real estate brokerage services for a buyer is the buyer's agent by operation of law unless the firm appointed that broker to the seller. The duties are statutory, not fiduciary (RCW 18.86.110). Beyond the duties owed to all parties in RCW 18.86.030, a buyer's agent owes the buyer loyalty, timely disclosure of conflicts, advice to seek expert help, confidentiality, and a good faith and continuous effort to find a property (RCW 18.86.050(1)).

questions.question_text: A seller's agent learns the buyer is willing to pay more than the listed price. What must the agent do?
questions.correct_answer: Disclose this information to the seller
distractors: Share it only if the buyer consents
Advise the buyer to lower the offer
questions.explanation: A seller's agent owes the seller the statutory duty of loyalty — to take no action adverse or detrimental to the seller's interest (RCW 18.86.040(1)(a)). Knowing the buyer would pay more is information the agent must use for, and share with, the seller, its principal.

questions.question_text: Under Washington law, a buyer's agent who discovers the seller is under financial pressure to sell quickly should share this with whom?
questions.explanation: A buyer's agent owes the statutory duty of loyalty to the buyer alone (RCW 18.86.050(1)(a)). The seller's time pressure strengthens the buyer's negotiating position, so the buyer's agent shares it with the buyer and not with the other side.

questions.question_text: Which Washington statute governs the creation and duties of agency relationships in real estate transactions?
questions.explanation: The Washington Real Estate Brokerage Relationships Act, chapter 18.86 RCW, establishes the types of agency relationships and the duties owed by brokers to their principals and to all parties.

questions.question_text: Under SB 5191 effective January 1, 2024, the term 'dual agency' was officially renamed to what in Washington?
questions.explanation: Washington renamed 'dual agency' to 'limited dual agency' under SB 5191, effective January 1, 2024, to better reflect the reduced representation each party receives when one firm represents both sides.

questions.question_text: A managing broker's firm has one broker representing the buyer and another representing the seller in the same transaction. Under SB 5191, what happens to the designated broker?
questions.explanation: Under SB 5191, in an intra-firm transaction where two brokers represent opposite sides, the designated broker and supervising managing brokers automatically become limited dual agents, even though the individual brokers continue representing their respective clients.

questions.question_text: Before entering a limited dual agency arrangement in Washington, what must be obtained from both the buyer and seller?
questions.explanation: Limited dual agency is permitted "only with the written consent of both parties to the transaction, set forth in the services agreement" (RCW 18.86.060(1)). Under RCW 18.86.020(2)(b)(iv) that consent must be separately initialed by the principal and include an acknowledgment that a limited dual agent may not advocate terms favorable to one principal to the detriment of the other.

questions.question_text: Broker Kim represents a buyer, and Broker Lee in the same firm represents the seller. Which description best identifies this situation under current Washington law?
questions.explanation: When two brokers within the same firm represent opposite parties, this creates an intra-firm limited dual agency situation under SB 5191. The designated broker and supervising managing brokers become limited dual agents while each broker continues representing their principal.

questions.question_text: In a limited dual agency arrangement, what is the primary impact on representation for each party?
questions.explanation: In limited dual agency neither party gets undivided advocacy. RCW 18.86.060(2)(a) reduces the loyalty duty to taking no action adverse or detrimental to either party, and the limited dual agent may not advocate terms favorable to one principal to the detriment of the other (RCW 18.86.020(2)(b)(iv)) — hence "limited" representation for each side.

questions.question_text: A broker representing the buyer discovers a known foundation crack in a property. Under Washington law, who must the broker inform?
distractors: Only the buyer as the principal
questions.explanation: A broker must disclose all existing material facts known to the broker and "not apparent or readily ascertainable to a party," and this duty runs to all parties regardless of whom the broker represents (RCW 18.86.030(1)(d)). It does not imply a duty to investigate: RCW 18.86.030(2) says the broker owes no duty to conduct an independent inspection. Note too that RCW 18.86.010(11) excludes murder, suicide, other death, sex or violent crime, robbery, drug or gang activity, and political or religious activity from the definition of a material fact.

questions.question_text: Which duty does a Washington broker owe to ALL parties in a real estate transaction, not just the principal?
questions.explanation: Dealing honestly and in good faith is one of the non-waivable duties RCW 18.86.030(1) owes to all parties. Loyalty, confidentiality, and advice to seek expert help are statutory duties owed only to the broker's principal (RCW 18.86.040(1)/.050(1)) — Washington has no separate obedience duty.

questions.question_text: A listing broker receives a written offer at 4:45 PM on Friday. The broker is leaving for vacation. What must the broker do?
questions.correct_answer: Present the offer to the seller timely
distractors: Hold it until a higher offer arrives
Forward it only if it is at full price
questions.explanation: Washington brokers must present all written offers and counteroffers to the appropriate party in a timely manner. This duty is owed to all parties regardless of representation and cannot be delayed for personal convenience.

questions.question_text: A broker receives earnest money from a buyer in a transaction. Which duty to all parties applies to these funds?
distractors: Invest the funds for maximum return
Deposit into a personal savings account
questions.explanation: Accounting for all money and property received is a duty owed to all parties under RCW 18.86. Brokers must properly track and safeguard all funds and property entrusted to them during a transaction.

questions.question_text: After a purchase agreement is signed by all parties, a Washington broker must provide what to each party?
questions.correct_answer: A copy of all signed documents
distractors: Only a verbal summary of terms
Documents only if the party requests
questions.explanation: Washington brokers owe a duty to all parties to provide copies of signed documents. This ensures all parties have records of the agreements they have entered into and is required regardless of whom the broker represents.

questions.question_text: A seller tells their listing broker they will accept $20,000 less than list price. What duty governs the broker's handling of this information?
distractors: Honesty and good faith to all
questions.explanation: Confidential information is information the principal reasonably expects to be kept confidential, has not authorized for disclosure, and that would operate to the principal's detriment if disclosed (RCW 18.86.010(9)). The seller's willingness to take less is exactly that, and RCW 18.86.040(1)(d) forbids the listing broker from disclosing it.

questions.question_text: After a listing agreement expires, a broker learns a former client is in foreclosure. Can the broker share this with a potential buyer?
distractors: Yes, the duty ended with the listing
Yes, if the buyer asks directly
questions.explanation: Confidential information may not be disclosed "except under subpoena or court order, even after termination of the agency relationship" (RCW 18.86.040(1)(d)), and after termination the only duties left are accounting for money and property and not disclosing confidential information (RCW 18.86.070(2)).

questions.question_text: A buyer's broker discovers a potential conflict of interest in a transaction. What must the broker do?
questions.correct_answer: Fully disclose the conflict to the buyer
distractors: Disclose only if asked by the buyer
Report the conflict to the DOL
questions.explanation: A buyer's agent must "timely disclose to the buyer any conflicts of interest" (RCW 18.86.050(1)(b)). That is an affirmative statutory duty — the broker must raise the conflict without waiting to be asked.

questions.question_text: A seller asks their broker to market a Seattle house only to a hand-picked group of buyers and not to the general public. What must the broker tell the seller?
questions.correct_answer: The property must be marketed to the public concurrently
distractors: The broker must follow the instruction
Only the designated broker may approve it
It is allowed if the seller signs a waiver
questions.explanation: A broker "may not market the sale or lease of residential real estate to a limited or exclusive group of prospective buyers or brokers" unless the property is concurrently marketed to the general public and all other brokers (RCW 18.86.130, added by SSB 6091 (2026 c 57) effective June 11, 2026). The only exception is what is reasonably necessary to protect the health or safety of the owner or occupant, and marketing to the public does not obligate the owner to allow anyone onto the property. Violating RCW 18.86.130 is a violation of RCW 18.85.361 (RCW 18.86.031).

questions.question_text: Which set of duties does a Washington broker owe ONLY to the principal, not to all parties?
questions.explanation: A closed list of duties is owed only to the principal: loyalty, timely disclosure of conflicts of interest, advice to seek expert help beyond the agent's expertise, confidentiality, and a good faith and continuous effort to find a buyer or property (RCW 18.86.040(1) and .050(1)). Honesty and good faith, reasonable skill and care, timely presentation of communications, material-fact disclosure, and accounting are owed to all parties under RCW 18.86.030. Washington has no obedience duty — RCW 18.86.110 replaced the common-law fiduciary framework with this statutory one.
